title: Tree Diagrams With and Without Replacement — Year 9

header.title: Tree Diagrams With and Without Replacement
header.subtitle: Multiply along a path, add across paths

meta.lesson-focus: Use tree diagrams to represent two- and three-step compound events; contrast experiments with and without replacement (e.g. drawing 3 cards from a deck); multiply probabilities along each path and sum across paths for the target event.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: list all outcomes for compound events both with and without replacement, using lists, tree diagrams, tables or arrays; assign probabilities to outcomes
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: The likelihood of an event occurring can be affected by another event that has already taken place

html.section0_intro: Last lesson you listed outcomes with lists and arrays. Today the experiments get longer, so we need a faster tool. These three questions check the skills you need: counting outcomes, multiplying fractions and adding fractions.
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's probability.

A café runs a lucky draw. A jar holds 3 gold and 7 silver tokens. Each customer draws two tokens and wins a $20 voucher if both are gold.

The owner must budget for the vouchers. But should the first token go back in the jar before the second draw, or stay out? That one decision changes the chance of winning, and so the cost per 300 customers.

A tree diagram shows each step of a compound event as a set of branches. Today you multiply along a path to find the probability of one outcome, and add across paths for an event that can happen more than one way. Without replacement, the second set of branches changes.

html.section3_desc: Drag each experiment into the right bucket. Ask: is anything removed before the next step?
html.sort_activity:
Sort each experiment by what happens on the second step
Roll a die twice Deal 2 cards from a deck Flip a coin three times Choose 3 students for a committee Spin a spinner twice Eat 2 chocolates from a box Draw a raffle ticket, put it back, draw again Draw 2 raffle winners from one barrel

Probabilities stay the same (with replacement)

Probabilities change (without replacement)

💡 Dice, coins and spinners have no memory: every roll or spin starts fresh. When something is taken away (a card dealt, a person chosen, a chocolate eaten) there is one fewer item for the next step.
html.section4_heading: Match the path to its probability
html.worked_example:
A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. Find P(one red and one blue).

1
Draw the tree and label every branch
First draw: 3 of 5 are red. If a red is taken out, 4 counters are left and only 2 are red. If a blue is taken out, 4 are left and 3 are red.
Each set of branches from one point adds to 1: 24 + 24 = 1 and 34 + 14 = 1
2
Multiply along each path
Each path is one outcome. Multiply the branch probabilities along it.
P(R, B) = 35 × 24 = 620   Check: 6 + 6 + 6 + 2 = 20, so the paths add to 1.
3
Add the paths that give the event
One of each colour happens two ways: red then blue, or blue then red.
P(one of each) = 620 + 620 = 1220 = 35

7bHinge check: two aces🎯 Pick one

Before you pick your tier: choose the correct working. Each wrong option hides a common mistake.

Two cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck without replacement. A deck has 4 aces. Which calculation gives P(both cards are aces)?
That is WITH replacement. The first ace is not put back, so the second branch has only 3 aces left out of 51 cards.
Multiply along a path, don't add. “Ace and then ace” is one path. Adding is only for combining different paths.
Correct. 452 × 351 = 122652 = 1221. Both the aces and the total drop by 1.
Half right. You removed an ace from the top, but the whole deck also shrinks: 52 − 1 = 51 cards are left.

retrieval.q: Two fair coins are flipped. What is P(two heads)? Type a fraction.
retrieval.hint: List HH, HT, TH, TT: only one is two heads.

fb.1/3: 0, 1 and 2 heads are not equally likely. Use the four outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT.

retrieval.q: Work out 35 × 24. Type a fraction.
retrieval.hint: Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms: 6/20, then simplify.

fb.5/9: That adds the tops and the bottoms. To multiply fractions, multiply numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator.

retrieval.q: Work out 16 + 13. Type a fraction.

fb.2/9: Denominators are not added. Make them the same first: 1/3 = 2/6.

weDo.q: Read the tree. What is P(the 1st pick is Year 9)? Type a fraction.
weDo.hint: 4 of the 10 members are in Year 9.

weDo.q: The 1st pick was Year 9. What is P(the 2nd pick is also Year 9)?
weDo.hint: One Year 9 student is gone: 3 Year 9 left out of 9 people.

fb.2/5: That is with replacement. The first student cannot be picked again, so 3 of 9 are Year 9.

weDo.q: Multiply along the top path. What is P(all three are Year 9)?

fb.8/125: That is (4/10)³, with replacement. Use 4/10, then 3/9, then 2/8.
fb.9/10: Add across different paths only. Along one path, multiply.

weDo.q: Three paths give exactly two Year 9 students: (Y9, Y9, Y10), (Y9, Y10, Y9) and (Y10, Y9, Y9). What is P(exactly two Year 9)?
weDo.hint: Each path is 72/720. Add the three paths: 216/720.

fb.1/10: That is only one of the three paths. The two Year 9 students can be picked in three different orders: add all three.

checkpoint.q: A bag holds 2 red and 3 blue counters. A counter is drawn, put back, and a second is drawn. What is P(R, R)?
checkpoint.hint: With replacement the branches stay the same: 2/5 × 2/5.

fb.1/10: That is without replacement. Here the first counter goes back, so the second draw is still 2 of 5.

checkpoint.q: The same bag of 2 red and 3 blue. This time the first counter is not put back. What is P(R, R)?
checkpoint.hint: 2/5, then only 1 red is left out of 4: 2/5 × 1/4.

fb.4/25: That is with replacement. After one red is removed there is 1 red out of 4.
fb.3/20: Both the reds and the total drop by 1: the second branch is 1/4.

practice1.hint: 2 branches, then 2 from each, then 2 from each: 2 × 2 × 2.

fb.6: Count the ends of the tree, not the branches in one column: 2 × 2 × 2 paths.

practice1.q: A coin is flipped three times. What is P(H, H, H)?

fb.3/2: Along a path you multiply, not add.

practice1.q: A fair die is rolled twice. What is P(two sixes)?

fb.1/3: That adds 1/6 + 1/6. Six and then six is one path: multiply.

practice1.q: A spinner lands on WIN with probability 13. It is spun twice. What is P(WIN, WIN)?
practice1.hint: Spins do not change the spinner: 1/3 × 1/3.

practice1.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters. One is drawn, put back, then a second is drawn.What is P(R, R)?

fb.2/15: That is without replacement. Here the counter goes back, so the branches stay 4/10.

practice1.q: Now the first counter is not put back.What is P(R, R)?

fb.4/25: That is with replacement. After a red is removed, 3 reds are left out of 9.

practice1.q: Same bag, without replacement. The first counter was red. What is P(the second is blue)?
practice1.hint: Read the branch after R: 6 blue out of 9 left.

fb.3/5: The total is now 9, not 10: one counter is out of the bag.

practice1.q: Same bag, without replacement. What is P(R then B)?
Same bag, without replacement. What is P(B, B)?

fb.9/25: That is with replacement: use 6/10 then 5/9.

practice1.q: Same bag, without replacement. What is P(one of each colour)?
practice1.hint: Add two paths: R then B (24/90) and B then R (24/90).

fb.4/15: That is only R then B. B then R also gives one of each: add both paths.

practice2.q: A coin is flipped three times. What is P(exactly two heads)?
practice2.hint: HHT, HTH and THH: three paths, each 1/8.

fb.1/8: That is one path. Two heads can happen in three orders: add HHT, HTH, THH.

practice2.q: A box has 5 caramel and 7 mint chocolates. Two are eaten at random. What is P(both caramel)?

fb.25/144: That is with replacement. An eaten chocolate does not come back: 5/12 × 4/11.

practice2.q: Same box. What is P(at least one mint)? Hint: use the complement.
practice2.hint: At least one mint = 1 − P(both caramel) = 1 − 5/33.

fb.5/33: That is P(both caramel), the opposite event. Subtract it from 1.

practice2.q: A school club has 20 members and 8 are in Year 9. Two members are chosen at random for a conference. What is P(both are Year 9)?

fb.4/25: That is with replacement. The same student cannot be chosen twice: 8/20 × 7/19.

practice2.q: A raffle has 50 tickets and you hold 1. Three prize tickets are drawn without replacement. What is P(you win nothing)?
Three cards are dealt from a 52-card deck without replacement. A deck has 13 hearts. What is P(all three are hearts)?

fb.1/64: That is with replacement, (1/4)³. Without replacement use 13/52, 12/51, 11/50.

practice3.q: Three cards are drawn from a 52-card deck with replacement. What is P(an ace, then the king of the same suit, then the queen of the same suit)?
practice3.hint: Any of the 4 aces: 4/52. Then only 1 king matches its suit: 1/52. Then 1 queen: 1/52.

fb.1/140608: The first card can be any of the 4 aces, so the first branch is 4/52, not 1/52.

practice3.q: The same three cards, but now without replacement. What is P(ace, then king, then queen, all the same suit)?

fb.1/35152: That is with replacement. The deck shrinks to 51, then 50 cards.

practice3.q: The café lucky draw: 3 gold and 7 silver tokens, two drawn without replacement, and a $20 voucher for two gold. How much should the café budget for vouchers per 300 customers, in dollars?

fb.540: That uses with replacement (9/100). The first token stays out: 3/10 × 2/9.

practice3.q: If the café puts the first token back before the second draw, how many more dollars of vouchers should it expect to give away per 300 customers?
practice3.hint: With replacement P = 3/10 × 3/10 = 9/100, so 27 winners = $540. Compare with $400.

fb.540: That is the new total. The question asks how much MORE than the $400 without replacement.

exitProbs.q: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(B, B)?

fb.4/25: That is with replacement. After one blue is gone, 1 blue is left out of 4.

exitProbs.q: The same bag, but the first counter is put back. What is P(B, B)?
Explain why the second set of branches in a tree diagram changes when you draw without replacement, but not with replacement.
exitProbs.hint: What happens to the number of items, and the number you want, after the first draw?
